title: The Promise

jokes.text: Now, that sign says 'applesauce.' No, I'm kidding. It says 'applause.'
jokes.setup: Hank is warming up the studio audience and points to the applause sign
jokes.punchline: He calls it 'applesauce' then immediately corrects himself — a deliberately lame misdirect that signals Hank's corny, self-satisfied sense of humor
jokes.explanation: The joke itself is groan-worthy but that's the point — it perfectly establishes Hank as the second banana who tells dad jokes with absolute confidence. Rewatch bonus because knowing Hank makes the corniness funnier in retrospect.

dialogue.speaker: Warm-up Comedian
dialogue.line: Now, that sign says 'applesauce.' No, I'm kidding. It says 'applause.'

jokes.text: In the event of a sudden loss of interest in one of tonight's guests, your seat cushion may be removed and used as a pillow.
jokes.setup: Karen is performing a straight airline safety briefing parody for the studio audience
jokes.punchline: The 'flotation device becomes pillow' gag reframes airline dullness as an admission that the show's guests might be boring — self-deprecating industry wit
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the sketch — the misdirect (safety briefing language) conceals a genuinely self-aware industry joke about boring talk show guests. The pillow twist is tight and the show-business subtext gives it extra flavor. Earned, economical, and specific.

dialogue.line: And now, because it's an F.A.A. Regulation... your flight attendant, Karen Jackson.

jokes.text: I think the only thing Karen forgot to add is please do not stand until we've come to a complete halt, which I think we just have.
jokes.setup: Larry takes the stage following the airline safety sketch
jokes.punchline: He extends the airline metaphor with the 'remain seated until a complete halt' callback — but the 'which I think we just have' addendum undercuts it with dry self-deprecation about the show starting
jokes.explanation: A solid callback that earns its place — Larry picking up the sketch's thread shows professional comedic awareness. The self-deprecating coda ('which I think we just have') is particularly sharp, suggesting the show is perpetually in motion and barely in control.

dialogue.line: To applaud, hold the hands out and away from the body... with the palms facing each other. Bring palms together firmly and quickly and continue to breathe normally.

jokes.text: We had another earthquake here in LA, and the bad thing about earthquakes when they happen in Los Angeles is it makes it more difficult to shoot straight.
jokes.setup: Larry brings up the recent LA earthquake as topical material
jokes.punchline: The punchline pivots to gun violence — LA earthquakes are bad because they make it harder to shoot people accurately
jokes.explanation: A decent dark twist on the topical-monologue format. The LA crime/violence subtext gives it some edge. It's not especially original as a structure but the specific LA stereotype makes it land.

dialogue.line: In the event of a sudden loss of interest in one of tonight's guests... your seat cushion may be removed and used as a pillow.

jokes.text: I was with my wife in bed at 5:00 a.m. and she started to yell, 'It's the big one.' And I said, 'Thank you very much.' And then she said, 'No, it's the quake.'
jokes.setup: Larry continues the earthquake monologue with a personal anecdote about being in bed with his wife
jokes.punchline: Wife's 'It's the big one' is initially misconstrued as a sexual compliment ('Thank you very much') before being clarified as earthquake terror
jokes.explanation: A classic misdirection joke — the sexual double meaning is well-executed structurally but relies on a well-worn template (the 'big one' earthquake/sex double entendre is not fresh). Gets laughs because the structure is airtight, but no points for originality.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I think the only thing Karen forgot to add... is please do not stand until we've come to a complete halt... which I think we just have.

jokes.text: Don't be like last night's audience. After the show was over, they laughed for an hour, they had fun with us for an hour, then they got dressed and just left.
jokes.setup: Larry addresses the audience about staying for the whole show
jokes.punchline: The audience's post-show behavior is described in terms of a one-night stand — 'had fun for an hour, then got dressed and just left'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the stronger monologue jokes — the sex-metaphor mapped onto audience behavior is genuinely novel for a talk show context, and it builds naturally into the 'I like to cuddle' follow-up. Garry Shandling's specific neurotic-host persona makes it land harder than it would from a generic host.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: the bad thing about earthquakes when they happen in Los Angeles... is it makes it more difficult to shoot straight.

jokes.text: Please, stay. I like to cuddle afterwards. And, you never know, an hour later I may feel like putting on another show.
jokes.setup: Larry has just compared the audience leaving after the show to a one-night stand
jokes.punchline: He extends the metaphor with 'I like to cuddle afterwards' and then the recovery-round joke about doing another show — escalating the sexual analogy to its absurd logical conclusion
jokes.explanation: The escalation here is elegant — 'I like to cuddle' is a great character-specific reveal (Larry as emotionally needy performer), and 'an hour later I may feel like putting on another show' is a crisp punch that extends the metaphor without belaboring it. High economy, strong character integration — Larry's neediness for audience approval is the subtext. This is the best joke of the monologue.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: she started to yell, 'It's the big one.' And I said, 'Thank you very much.' And then she said, 'No, it's the quake.'

jokes.text: What do I do now? / Just pretend like you're talking to me till we're off the air, so it won't seem weird.
jokes.setup: The show has just wrapped its on-air segment; Larry and Hank are filling dead air
jokes.punchline: Larry asks what to do; Hank instructs him to 'just pretend like you're talking' — a meta-admission that all post-interview desk chat is performative filler
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp piece of showbiz deconstruction — the artifice of late-night talk shows laid bare in two lines. The Larry Sanders Show's entire thesis is in this joke. The instruction to 'pretend' while the cameras are still rolling is both funny and quietly damning. Strong rewatch value as a thesis-statement moment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: After the show was over, they laughed for an hour... they had fun with us for an hour, then they got dressed and just left.

jokes.text: My house? I'm in a lawsuit with the contractor because the walls are bleeding like a miracle.
jokes.setup: Larry asks Hank how his house is coming along to fill dead air
jokes.punchline: Hank's contractor situation escalates immediately and surreally to 'walls bleeding like a miracle' — delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The phrase 'bleeding like a miracle' is a perfect comic construction — miracles bleed, bleeding is bad, and Hank deploys both associations simultaneously with zero ironic distance. The deadpan delivery implied by Tambor's Hank persona makes it funnier. High originality: this construction is specific and strange in a way that feels genuinely inspired. Larry's flat 'That's great' in response is the ideal button.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Please, stay. I like to cuddle afterwards. And, you never know, an hour later I may feel like putting on another show.

jokes.text: Give me a speed-through. / The whole joke? / Please. / This is an office, not a club.
jokes.setup: Jerry asks Spade to run through his airline material
jokes.punchline: Spade protests 'This is an office, not a club' — a comedian's instinctive resistance to performing out of context, which is both relatable and slightly precious
jokes.explanation: A nice little character-specific resistance — Spade's comedian vanity showing through. 'This is an office, not a club' is a quotable line with some life to it. Shows real insider knowledge of how stand-ups think about material.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Sleep well. Remember, we'll all be sleeping at the same time.

jokes.text: David Spade's airline stand-up material: 'They immediately tell you the name of your pilot. Like anyone goes, Oh, he's good. I like his work.'
jokes.setup: Flying-fear setup: airlines tell you the pilot's name as reassurance
jokes.punchline: Nobody has opinions about pilots the way they have opinions about artists — 'I like his work' is the wrong register entirely
jokes.explanation: Spade's actual stand-up material — competent observational comedy with a solid misdirection ('I like his work' vs. what you'd say about a pilot). Above-average stand-up, helped by the specific phrasing.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.line: My house? I'm in a lawsuit with the contractor... because the walls are bleeding like a miracle.

jokes.text: In coach, they don't want you to see the people in first class. That's how much of a loser you are. And the flight attendant will come by and pull the curtain shut. 'Sorry.'
jokes.setup: Spade riffs on flying coach vs. first class
jokes.punchline: The curtain pull with 'Sorry' — the flight attendant's gesture as an act of class-based condescension delivered with maximum politeness
jokes.explanation: The best of Spade's actual stand-up material here. The curtain-pull 'Sorry' is economical, the class dynamics observation is sharp, and 'that's how much of a loser you are' is a well-timed escalation. Above-average stand-up.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: This is an office, not a club. David, I know this is total torture... but you gotta do your act for me so Larry can hear the content.

jokes.text: Then I do my dog's penis... / Did you say 'penis'? / I say 'penis.' I can change it to 'organ.'
jokes.setup: Spade is running through his act; the conversation is matter-of-fact and businesslike
jokes.punchline: The clinical mid-pitch mention of 'dog's penis' jolts the room; Spade's offer to substitute 'organ' (which is arguably worse) is the secondary laugh
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from the contrast between the bureaucratic tone of the pre-show review and Spade casually dropping 'dog's penis' mid-sentence. 'I can change it to organ' is a funny instinct — organ is no more acceptable, just more pretentious.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Like anyone goes, 'Oh, he's good. I like his work.'

jokes.text: You will not change a thing. That's what this show needs — penis, and plenty of it.
jokes.setup: Jerry had seemed squeamish about the word 'penis'; Spade offered to change it
jokes.punchline: Jerry reverses completely — not only is 'penis' fine, it's apparently the show's salvation. The hyperbolic endorsement is a character-specific joke about network/producer anxiety over content
jokes.explanation: A very good reversal — Jerry's sudden evangelical enthusiasm for 'penis, and plenty of it' is both funny as a line and a sharp satire of TV producers who perform prudishness before overcorrecting into permissiveness. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.line: And the flight attendant will come by and pull the curtain shut. 'Sorry.'

jokes.text: Larry enters, tells Spade he's excited about Star Trek thing, then leaves. Jerry tells Spade: 'You can't say penis.' / 'Got it.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just breezed through, told Spade 'penis' is fine and he's like family — all warmth and enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: The moment Larry leaves, Jerry reverses the ruling on 'penis' — the power hierarchy is instantly clarified; everything Larry said was performative
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best structural jokes — a three-beat reversal that comments on the entire backstage power dynamic of late-night TV. Larry performs magnanimity; the moment he exits, reality reasserts. The callback to 'penis' works as the specific test case. The structure is near-perfect: setup (Jerry's enthusiasm), complication (Larry's entrance and override), punchline (the instant reversal). Strong character integration — this could only happen in a show about the gap between on-air persona and behind-the-scenes reality.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: You make that little face? That is so Spade, and Larry loves that.

jokes.text: Larry's awkward office visit with a young comedian — stilted small talk, premature goodbye, confusion over 'So long' / 'Long?', then Larry watching him leave: 'Nice kid.'
jokes.setup: Larry invited a young comedian to 'stop by,' clearly not having planned what to say. The visit consists entirely of hollow affirmations ('Things are going well, huh?' / 'Good.' / 'I'm really very glad.') before Larry awkwardly wraps it up.
jokes.punchline: 'Nice kid' — delivered to himself after the door closes — is the entire point: Larry has no relationship with this person and the visit meant nothing. The vacancy of showbiz mentorship in three syllables.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest sustained comedic sequences. The scene is almost entirely void of content — that IS the content. Larry's hollow encouragements ('Everything is going great' / 'Very glad. I'm really very glad') are excavated of all meaning, and 'Nice kid' as the internal verdict after a pointless interaction is perfectly calibrated Larry Sanders characterization. The 'So long/Long?' beat is a small gem of miscommunication cringe. Could only be this character in this show. Rewatch bonus: you notice how little Larry actually listens.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: You will not. You will not change a thing. That's what this show needs... penis, and plenty of it.

jokes.text: So, you still driving the... The Hon... No, I've got a new Mustang. It's brand-new. / Those are great. I love those.
jokes.setup: Larry has invited Spade to his office for a friendly chat — but has nothing to actually say
jokes.punchline: Larry can't even remember what car Spade used to drive; Spade pivots; Larry fills with generic enthusiasm ('Those are great. I love those'). The conversation is pure hollow celebrity small talk
jokes.explanation: This is pure Shandling cringe — Larry invited Spade in as a social gesture but has zero actual interest in him as a person. The aborted Honda question, the pivot to Mustang, and Larry's reflexive 'Those are great, I love those' is a devastating portrait of celebrity-to-celebrity interaction as performance. High character integration: this is quintessentially Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: How many times you been on, Paula?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Never.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Exactly. So show Mr. Spade here a little respect.

jokes.text: I guess it's that time. / Long? / So long. I'm gonna go drive the Mustang. / Those are great. Have fun.
jokes.setup: The conversation between Larry and Spade has hit a wall of awkward emptiness
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'I guess it's that time' is interrupted by Spade mishearing 'long' — the stumble perfectly encapsulates how eager both are to end the interaction. 'I'm gonna go drive the Mustang' as an exit line is beautifully mundane.
jokes.explanation: The 'Long/So long' mishearing is brilliant in its simplicity — both characters are so desperate to end this that Spade hears 'long?' in the middle of a word, and the callback to the Mustang ('I'm gonna go drive the Mustang') as his excuse to flee is perfect situational comedy. The whole scene is a masterclass in comedic awkwardness.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: You can't say 'penis.' Got it.

jokes.text: Nice kid.
jokes.setup: Spade has just left after one of the most hollow celebrity interactions imaginable
jokes.punchline: Larry's flat 'Nice kid' is the button — the total inadequacy of the assessment relative to what we've witnessed
jokes.explanation: Two words that do enormous work. 'Nice kid' is perfectly calibrated — it conveys that Larry has filed Spade away as irrelevant while feeling vaguely warm about it. The economy is near-perfect. It's the ideal button for the scene.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: The Hon... No, I've got a new Mustang. It's brand-new.

jokes.text: Put on Leno, honey. Please?
jokes.setup: Larry is on the phone with his wife at home; he's just been told Artie called — we're eavesdropping on a private domestic moment
jokes.punchline: Larry, the host of a competing late-night show, casually asks his wife to put on Leno — the professional rival he will soon be furious at for stealing Spade
jokes.explanation: A nicely planted irony — Larry watching Leno is both believable (hosts watch their competition obsessively) and sets up the explosion to come. The domestic casualness of 'Put on Leno, honey. Please?' is perfect character texture.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I guess it's that time. Thanks for coming by.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: So... Long? So long.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: I'm gonna go drive the Mustang.

jokes.text: Larry watches Leno and discovers David Spade performing the exact airline material he just previewed for the Larry Sanders show.
jokes.setup: Larry asked his wife to put on Leno casually; the Spade situation seems dormant
jokes.punchline: Spade appears on Leno doing literally the material he just ran through for the Larry Sanders show — the betrayal is visualized in real time as Larry watches
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's structural masterstroke. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) the callback to the material we literally just heard previewed, (2) the situational irony of Larry putting on Leno himself, (3) the dramatic escalation as the penny drops. The earned quality is extremely high — this has been built across the episode's first half. One of the standout moments. The craft in the structure alone justifies an 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Nice kid.

jokes.text: I thought he was doing our show tomorrow, Artie. What the fuck is this?
jokes.setup: Larry has just seen Spade on Leno doing the exact material previewed for his show
jokes.punchline: Larry's explosion — 'What the fuck is this?' — is both the righteous indignation of the wronged host and the petulance of a man who invited Spade into his office hours ago and called him a 'nice kid'
jokes.explanation: The explosive reaction is largely carried by context — the irony of Larry's position (he liked Spade 40 minutes ago; called him 'nice kid') makes the outrage funnier than it reads. Solid character beat, well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I am not allowed to talk about show business, Artie. Put on Leno, honey. Please?

jokes.text: You don't do two talk shows back-to-back. It's an unspoken rule. / Maybe it's so unspoken that he didn't know about it.
jokes.setup: Larry is furious; his wife tries to offer perspective
jokes.punchline: Wife's dry 'Maybe it's so unspoken that he didn't know about it' is the perfect deflating response — calling out that 'unspoken rules' are a convenient fiction
jokes.explanation: A wonderful piece of dry wit — the wife punctures Larry's outrage with a logically airtight observation. 'Unspoken rules' as a concept is inherently absurd, and she names the absurdity without Larry being able to refute it. The structure (indignant declaration / logical deflation) is clean and satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I thought he was doing our show tomorrow, Artie. What the fuck is this?

jokes.text: I sound like an asshole. / No, honey. You don't sound like an asshole. Your feelings are hurt. / My feelings are hurt, honey, and by a man.
jokes.setup: Larry is mid-rant about Spade's betrayal, invoking the language of loyalty and discovery
jokes.punchline: 'My feelings are hurt, honey, and by a man' — the absurd specificity of 'and by a man' as though this particular grievance is categorically more shameful or confusing
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best lines and a genuine standout. 'My feelings are hurt, honey, and by a man' perfectly crystallizes Larry's specific brand of masculine emotional confusion — he can process the betrayal, but the source (another man) adds a layer of shame and bewilderment he can't articulate. It's deeply character-specific (only Larry Sanders would say this), quotable, and gets funnier the more you think about what it reveals. High marks across originality, character integration, and earned quality.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You don't do two talk shows back-to-back. It's an unspoken rule. Maybe it's so unspoken that he didn't know about it.

jokes.text: Book Nell Carter on the show. We'll lock her in her dressing room for three days and don't feed her. Then throw David Spade in there with a piece of HoneyBaked ham down his pants. Stand back and thank me later.
jokes.setup: The team is figuring out how to retaliate against Spade; Artie says 'we're going to rise above it'
jokes.punchline: Paula ignores 'rising above it' and delivers an elaborate, violent revenge fantasy involving Nell Carter and HoneyBaked ham
jokes.explanation: Wildly specific and escalating — the three-day starvation plan, the HoneyBaked ham detail, the 'stand back and thank me later' confidence. The specificity of 'HoneyBaked ham' is what elevates it from generic dark joke to inspired absurdism. Paula's delivery of this as a serious professional proposal is perfect. One of the episode's most quotable moments.

dialogue.line: Maybe it's so unspoken that he didn't know about it.

jokes.text: Can we get Nell Carter? / I can get Nell Carter. If I can't, I'm gonna dress up like Nell Carter and kick his ass myself.
jokes.setup: The Nell Carter revenge plan is being evaluated for feasibility
jokes.punchline: Paula's contingency plan — personally dressing as Nell Carter to kick Spade — is both an absurdist escalation and a statement of professional commitment
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'book Nell Carter' to 'I will personally become Nell Carter' is beautifully insane. Paula's can-do attitude applied to revenge cosplay is a great character beat. The line lands because of its complete commitment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: My feelings are hurt, honey, and by a man.

jokes.text: All those years in the merchant marine have served you well, Paula.
jokes.setup: Paula has just offered to dress as Nell Carter and physically assault David Spade
jokes.punchline: Artie's response treats her violent competence as the natural outcome of a seafaring past — the non-sequitur explanation delivered as absolute fact
jokes.explanation: One of Rip Torn's best line deliveries in the episode. The joke works because it does two things at once: it tells us something absurd about Paula's past (merchant marine!) and it treats her violent proposal as merely the expression of a relevant skill set. The economy is exceptional — nine words of dialogue that land like a short story. This is distinctly Artie: gruff, strange, matter-of-fact.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Book Nell Carter on the show. We'll lock her in her dressing room for three days and don't feed her. Then throw David Spade in there with a piece of HoneyBaked ham down his pants.

jokes.text: Do you want me to make Spade fall in love with me, then hurt him? / He can. / No. Thanks, though.
jokes.setup: The group is brainstorming revenge against Spade after his Tonight Show betrayal
jokes.punchline: A staffer volunteers to seduce and emotionally destroy Spade — Artie immediately endorses it; Larry declines politely ('No. Thanks, though')
jokes.explanation: A superb three-beat joke that hinges entirely on the 'No. Thanks, though' — the politeness of the refusal in context is the joke. Artie's instant 'He can' adds perfect comic rhythm. The economy is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: All those years in the merchant marine have served you well, Paula.

jokes.text: By the way, Lenny and Squiggy say hi.
jokes.setup: The staffer's Lenny and Squiggy reference comes as a non-sequitur button to the love-trap proposal
jokes.punchline: The implication that this person is personally acquainted with the Laverne & Shirley characters — or the actors who played them — delivered as a throwaway
jokes.explanation: An insider Hollywood name-drop that lands as a mild chuckle. The implication (seduction skills acquired through Laverne & Shirley-adjacent social circles?) is vague but charming. Weaker than the surrounding jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: If I can't, I'm gonna dress up like Nell Carter and kick his ass myself.

jokes.text: I was so upset last night, I had to take a Halcion. / Aren't there side effects to that stuff, Artie? / Sure. I saw Buddy Ebsen's head floating over my dresser. But he vanished. Slept like a dream.
jokes.setup: The team is processing their collective outrage; Larry mentions needing sleep medication
jokes.punchline: Artie's Halcion hallucination: Buddy Ebsen's disembodied head floating over his dresser — reported with complete equanimity as a minor side effect
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best line. 'I saw Buddy Ebsen's head floating over my dresser. But he vanished. Slept like a dream.' works on every level: (1) Buddy Ebsen is an inspired choice — specific, B-list-celebrity-surreal, not too famous to be absurd; (2) 'But he vanished' is the perfect mid-beat reassurance; (3) 'Slept like a dream' is the deadpan button that implies the floating head was a mild inconvenience. This is quintessential Artie — experienced, unflappable, and casually disturbing. Only Rip Torn's Artie could deliver this. Among the best jokes in the episode by any measure.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Do you want me to make Spade fall in love with me, then hurt him?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: He can.

jokes.text: He was in here last night. / Where? Here? / In here. / What's he doing in here? / I asked him to stop by. / Why? / I thought it was a nice thing to say. / I didn't know he'd actually do it. / You mean come in here? / Yes. / Amazing.
jokes.setup: Artie is furious about Spade's betrayal; Larry reveals Spade was actually IN HIS OFFICE last night
jokes.punchline: Larry invited Spade in as an empty social gesture — 'I didn't know he'd actually do it' — the revelation that celebrity niceties are never meant to be taken literally, and Larry's genuine shock that Spade did
jokes.explanation: A devastating callback — we SAW the office visit, and now we learn Larry never actually wanted Spade to show up. 'I thought it was a nice thing to say' and 'I didn't know he'd actually do it' perfectly encapsulate the phoniness of showbiz friendliness. Artie's 'Amazing' is the ideal dry button. High character integration — this is specifically about Larry's inability to mean anything he says to guests.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: By the way, Lenny and Squiggy say hi.

jokes.text: I'm surprised you didn't smell Leno's cologne on the little rat bastard.
jokes.setup: Artie is cataloguing Spade's treacheries — he taped Tonight Show before coming to see Larry
jokes.punchline: The image of Spade carrying Leno's cologne on him as evidence of the betrayal — framed as detective work Larry should have performed
jokes.explanation: Artie's line casts the Spade situation as a noir betrayal — the cologne as evidence of infidelity is a great metaphor that gives the corporate backstabbing a more visceral, personal texture. 'Little rat bastard' is perfectly calibrated Artie invective.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Sure. I saw Buddy Ebsen's head floating over my dresser. But he vanished. Slept like a dream.

jokes.text: Fuck him. He's off the show. / I thought it'd take you another ten minutes. / What are you gonna do now? / Wanna get something to eat?
jokes.setup: Larry has been building to banning Spade from the show
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'I thought it'd take you another ten minutes' shows he predicted this outcome all along, then immediately pivots to 'Wanna get something to eat?' — the anticlimactic domesticity after all the drama
jokes.explanation: The genius is in Artie's casual calibration of Larry's emotional timeline. He's so familiar with Larry's patterns that he can predict the exact emotional arc. Then immediately: 'Wanna get something to eat?' — the mundane deflation of everything they've just been through. Very Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'm surprised you didn't smell Leno's cologne on the little rat bastard.

jokes.text: Listen, wasn't Karen great in that stewardess sketch last night? / No, Hank. No matter what she did to you, we're not having her back.
jokes.setup: Hank brings up Karen's performance in the sketch with apparent innocence
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately sees through Hank's gambit — this is clearly a relationship play, not a professional assessment — and shuts it down with 'No matter what she did to you'
jokes.explanation: A lovely double-layered joke — Hank attempts a transparent ploy; Artie dismantles it instantly. 'No matter what she did to you' is doing a lot of work: it implies history, bad behavior, and Artie's weary knowledge of Hank's romantic life. Strong character integration for both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: My pal Ray Combs hosts Family Feud, he's getting her on his show for me. Is that right?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Great. Her and her family?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, just her.

jokes.text: Sometimes when they have a family with just four people, they slap on a fifth person and make them a cousin or whatever. / They do that? / Hush-hush.
jokes.setup: Hank explains that Ray Combs is getting Karen onto Family Feud; Artie notes families usually have five
jokes.punchline: Hank reveals that Family Feud apparently manufactures fake cousins to complete undersized families — delivered as insider knowledge with a conspiratorial 'Hush-hush'
jokes.explanation: A very funny piece of showbiz-insider absurdism — the idea that Family Feud quietly fabricates family members is simultaneously plausible and insane. Hank's 'Hush-hush' treating it as classified information is perfect. The joke works because it sounds like it might be true.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Sometimes when they have a family with just four people... they slap on a fifth person and make them a cousin or whatever. They do that? Hush-hush.

jokes.text: The regional presidents of the Hank Kingsley Fan Club are visiting the studio and I throw a little wingding.
jokes.setup: Hank is asking Larry for a favor — to say a few words to some visitors
jokes.punchline: The Hank Kingsley Fan Club has regional presidents — the organizational formality applied to a fan club for a second banana sidekick is inherently absurd
jokes.explanation: Deeply Hank — the idea that his fan club has regional presidents implies a national infrastructure. The absurdity is underscored by the fact that it's a fan club for the sidekick, not the host. 'I throw a little wingding' is a wonderful Hank-ism.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Can't you hear my voice that I'm saying no to you? Please? I'm saying no. We're such good friends, and you can't hear that I'm saying no to you?

jokes.text: Can't you hear my voice that I'm saying no to you? / Please? / I'm saying no. / We're such good friends, and you can't hear that I'm saying no to you? / Don't make me say the words. / Please? / No! For God's sakes, no, Hank! You talk to you, and you don't hear!
jokes.setup: Hank is asking Larry to briefly say hello to the fan club; Larry keeps declining; Hank keeps asking
jokes.punchline: 'You talk to you, and you don't hear!' — Larry's exasperated mangling of the idiom ('you talk to yourself and you don't listen') in his frustration, which perfectly captures the breakdown of their dynamic
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Larry's frustration to the point of grammatical incoherence is a great cringe escalation — 'You talk to you, and you don't hear!' is wrong in a way that perfectly conveys the texture of real exasperation. The sustained 'please'/'no' loop beforehand creates the right tension. Strong character integration for both — Hank's oblivious persistence vs. Larry's unraveling politeness.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No! For God's sakes, no, Hank! You talk to you, and you don't hear!

jokes.text: Why is Larry so mean? What is he, 'Sadge'? / Larry can do what he wants to do. Spade really hurt his feelings.
jokes.setup: Darlene has heard that Spade is off the show and is puzzled by Larry's reaction
jokes.punchline: 'Sadge' — an astrological portmanteau for sad/Sagittarius — as an explanation for Larry's behavior. Artie's patient 'Spade really hurt his feelings' is the straight-man button
jokes.explanation: A mild character joke — Darlene's astrological framework as an explanation for complex emotional behavior is a nice character tic. 'Sadge' is a decent portmanteau. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: Why is Larry so mean? What is he, 'Sadge'?

jokes.text: Hank's fan club newsletter: 'Hank's For The Memories'
jokes.setup: Darlene is making copies of Hank's fan club newsletter
jokes.punchline: The newsletter title 'Hank's For The Memories' — a pun on 'Thanks for the Memories' (Bob Hope's theme song) — read aloud by Darlene as she handles the copies
jokes.explanation: A very economical joke — one newsletter title does multiple things: establishes Hank's showbiz pretensions (referencing a Bob Hope classic), his vanity, and the slight melancholy of the 'memories' framing for a current sidekick. The pun is groan-worthy in a good way. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: Try and get him to say 'Klingon.'

jokes.text: Jerry, William Shatner's on line four for you. / He wants to talk to me? / Yes. / Could we put him on the speakerphone? / Yeah, I love his voice.
jokes.setup: Shatner has called about the sketch; normally the assistant would just patch him through
jokes.punchline: Jerry's instant enthusiasm for speakerphone is explicitly because he loves Shatner's voice — the celebrity worship among the behind-the-scenes staff punctures the professional veneer
jokes.explanation: A cute moment of showbiz reality — the staffers are star-struck even by Shatner, and the speakerphone as a way to share the experience is endearing and satirical simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: The handset's broken, but we're alone.

jokes.text: Try and get him to say 'Klingon.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is excited to have Shatner on speakerphone
jokes.punchline: Darlene's specific request — 'Klingon' — reduces William Shatner to a human novelty sound machine
jokes.explanation: Five words that are perfectly observed. Darlene doesn't want to hear a story, doesn't want insight — she wants Shatner to say 'Klingon.' The economy is near-perfect. Funny because it's exactly what everyone would want but no professional would admit.

dialogue.speaker: Shatner
dialogue.line: Isn't Star Trek the most obvious, unoriginal choice you could make? I mean, come on.

jokes.text: Mr. Shatner, I'm gonna put you on speakerphone. / Yeah, Jerry. Am I on a speakerphone? / The handset's broken, but we're alone.
jokes.setup: Jerry told Shatner he'd be on speakerphone; Shatner immediately clocks it
jokes.punchline: Jerry's transparent lie — 'The handset's broken, but we're alone' — while an entire room of people listens
jokes.explanation: A satisfying situational irony — the audience knows the room is full of people; Shatner probably knows; Jerry's lie is transparent. The specific cover story ('handset's broken') is a funny detail. The deadpan commitment to the lie makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm really excited about doing this Star Trek thing the guys have written.

jokes.text: Isn't Star Trek the most obvious, unoriginal choice you could make? I mean, come on.
jokes.setup: The team has pitched a Star Trek sketch to Shatner
jokes.punchline: Shatner dismisses Star Trek as 'the most obvious, unoriginal choice' — the man most associated with Star Trek complaining about Star Trek as an obvious choice is a perfect meta-irony
jokes.explanation: This is a high-craft joke — it requires Shatner's specific cultural baggage to land, and it lands perfectly. The audacity of Captain Kirk calling Star Trek 'the most obvious, unoriginal choice' is both satirical (Shatner's exhaustion with his own legacy) and structurally elegant (the man who IS Star Trek dismissing it). The meta-self-referential quality is exceptional. Only improves with knowledge of Shatner's career.

dialogue.speaker: Shatner
dialogue.line: DeForest Kelley and I had some problems. I mean alien-wise.

jokes.text: Bill, this is Larry. / Larry! How you been? / Good. I was walking by and heard your voice on the speakerphone. I thought I'd pop in 'cause I'm really excited about doing this Star Trek thing the guys have written. / Great! A Star Trek sketch! That'll be fun!
jokes.setup: Shatner has just called Star Trek 'the most obvious, unoriginal choice'; now Larry butts in
jokes.punchline: Larry's enthusiasm ('I'm really excited about doing this Star Trek thing') instantly reverses Shatner's position — he goes from dismissive to 'Great! That'll be fun!' the moment the host himself endorses it
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's finest joke structurally. In two exchanges, Shatner goes from 'most obvious, unoriginal choice' to 'Great! That'll be fun!' the moment Larry's name enters the room. It's a devastating satire of celebrity sycophancy and the power of the host — all Shatner's intellectual posturing evaporates instantly. The structure (dismissal / immediate reversal upon power-shift) is textbook situational comedy executed flawlessly. Character integration is exceptional: this could only happen in a show about the machinery of celebrity.

dialogue.speaker: Shatner
dialogue.line: What's so funny?

jokes.text: Say, Bill? / Yeah? / What was your biggest enemy on Star Trek? / DeForest Kelley and I had some problems.
jokes.setup: Larry asks Shatner about his 'biggest enemy on Star Trek' — clearly meaning alien enemies from the show
jokes.punchline: Shatner interprets it as a personal question about cast conflicts and names DeForest Kelley — a real on-set rivalry
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed misdirection — the question is framed as fictional (alien enemies) but Shatner answers personally (real co-star beef). It works because: (1) it's entirely plausible for Shatner to have taken it that way, (2) the DeForest Kelley name-drop is specific enough to feel true, (3) the setup/misdirect structure is efficient and clean. 'I mean alien-wise' is the perfect clarification punchline. One of the episode's most quotable exchanges.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You're a married woman, but don't tempt me.

jokes.text: I mean alien-wise. / Who were the evil aliens who were always after you? / Romulans. There were some Romulans. / Klingons. There were some Klingons.
jokes.setup: Larry has clarified he meant alien enemies; Shatner recalls
jokes.punchline: Shatner's 'Romulans. There were some Romulans. Klingons. There were some Klingons.' — the deliberately vague, almost bored recollection of his own show's iconic villains, and 'Klingon' being said naturally
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Darlene's 'try and get him to say Klingon' — it happens naturally, not forced, which is the best possible callback delivery. Shatner's deadpan 'There were some Klingons' treats his own mythology with casual indifference. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: When they respect you too much, there's... there's a distance.

jokes.text: What's so funny? [Shatner asks, as the room erupts in laughter they can't explain]
jokes.setup: The room has burst into laughter — presumably at the Klingon payoff and Shatner's oblivious delivery
jokes.punchline: Shatner is completely unaware of what's funny — the gap between his self-seriousness and their delight
jokes.explanation: A perfect button — Shatner's 'What's so funny?' confirms his complete unawareness and extends the joke. The economy is exceptional (four words). The character integration is high: Shatner-as-oblivious-icon is a rich comedic concept.

dialogue.speaker: Ray
dialogue.line: Applesauce!

jokes.text: And this is where they make me beautiful.
jokes.setup: Hank is conducting a fan club tour of the studio; he's showing them the makeup room
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'This is where they make me beautiful' — the implication that he requires professional intervention to achieve presentability
jokes.explanation: A standard self-deprecating studio-tour quip. Works on a functional level but relies on an extremely common template. Not special.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I haven't heard this many women applaud since my bris.

jokes.text: You're beautiful enough as it is, Hank. / You're a married woman, but don't tempt me.
jokes.setup: A fan compliments Hank after his makeup room quip
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'You're a married woman, but don't tempt me' — the performative flirtation of the aging sidekick
jokes.explanation: A fairly generic flirty-sidekick line. Hank's vanity and mild desperation are present but the joke itself is well-worn. Functions as character texture rather than an actual comedic highlight.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I know it isn't, but if people could see Hank, who would look at me?

jokes.text: Now here comes one of our writers. Now this is Phil. Hey now, Phil! / ... / How's it going, Phil? / Now you see that? It's very sad. When they respect you too much, there's... there's a distance.
jokes.setup: Hank excitedly introduces the writer Phil to his fan club during the studio tour
jokes.punchline: Phil responds with awkward silence / minimal acknowledgment; Hank interprets this as 'too much respect' creating distance — a profound misread of what is clearly mild disdain or indifference
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character comedy moments. Hank's reframe of a writer's cold shoulder as 'too much respect' is a brilliant piece of psychological self-protection — and Tambor's delivery of 'It's very sad... when they respect you too much, there's a distance' needs to be played with utter sincerity to work. This is foundational Hank Kingsley characterization: the man who cannot perceive his own irrelevance. The gap between Hank's self-image and reality is the engine of the show's sadder comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Knock, knock.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Who's there?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You said, 'Knock, knock.'

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, I was just... I was just saying that.

jokes.text: You see that? It's very sad. When they respect you too much, there's... there's a distance.
jokes.setup: A writer has just completely ignored Hank in front of the fan club
jokes.punchline: Hank reframes the snub as a compliment — 'they respect you too much, there's a distance' — to save face in front of the fans
jokes.explanation: Jeffrey Tambor's greatest moment in the episode. The absurd reframe — transforming humiliation into a form of respect — is both funny and deeply sad. 'When they respect you too much, there's a distance' is a genuinely quotable line that captures the pathetic dignity Hank maintains at all times. This is Hank's defining character trait expressed in one perfect sentence. The pause before 'there's a distance' suggests Hank is inventing this rationalization in real time. Very high craft and high impact.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: How do you think Merv felt?

jokes.text: Applesauce!
jokes.setup: Hank is touring his fan club through the studio; they reach the spot where the applause signs are used
jokes.punchline: Hank says 'Applesauce!' — a callback to his opening warm-up joke — delivered with the self-satisfied energy of a man who considers this a signature bit
jokes.explanation: The callback works specifically because Hank is treating a throwaway warm-up gag as a signature piece. The fan club's presumably enthusiastic response (implied) is itself the joke. This is Hank treating a groan-worthy bit as precious — perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Jesus, Merv must have been pissed off.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: He was not pissed off. They were on at different times of the day.

jokes.text: Hank, you didn't tell me there'd be babes.
jokes.setup: A male crew member encounters the fan club (apparently all women) during the tour
jokes.punchline: The buddy-ish, slightly objectifying 'you didn't tell me there'd be babes' — puncturing the professional tour atmosphere
jokes.explanation: A weak joke — the 'babes' line is generic and doesn't add character specificity or satirical value. It's filler that establishes the fan club is female, which the show could have done more elegantly.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hey, call me...

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: You want me to call you?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I was gonna say, 'Call me Larry.'

jokes.text: I haven't heard this many women applaud since my bris.
jokes.setup: Larry has been ambushed by Hank's fan club in the studio; they applaud his appearance
jokes.punchline: The bris comparison — the only other time women applauded Larry in such numbers was at his ritual circumcision — a darkly absurd, specifically Jewish, specifically Larry joke
jokes.explanation: A standout line — the bris joke is perfectly specific. The construction is tight (women applauding → bris as the benchmark comparison), the Jewish self-deprecation is authentic to Shandling's persona, and the dark absurdism (celebrating genital surgery) adds an edge. 'Since my bris' is such a specific, strange choice that it registers as genuinely original. One of the episode's most quotable moments.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hey, call me... You want me to call you? I was gonna say, 'Call me Larry.'

jokes.text: Why does Hank have to sit so far down on the sofa? We can barely see him. It's not right. / I know it isn't, but if people could see Hank, who would look at me?
jokes.setup: A fan club member complains about Hank's positioning on the show's couch — too far from center to be properly seen
jokes.punchline: Larry's candid admission: he deliberately positions Hank poorly because Larry needs to be the visual focus — said directly to Hank's fans with zero self-consciousness
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy — Larry's complete lack of pretense with Hank's fans is a devastating portrait of the host-sidekick power dynamic. 'If people could see Hank, who would look at me?' is said to the people who are there specifically for Hank. The audacity is the joke. This is Larry's character at its most bracingly honest: self-centered, but so openly that it circles back around to charming. High marks across character integration, economy, and earned quality.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I gave him that whole manager/agent shit. And he bought it?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Of course. He said it was his manager and agent?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's what he told me. You bought that horseshit?

jokes.text: What's my name again? / Larry!
jokes.setup: Larry has just admitted he deliberately keeps Hank sidelined; the fans called his name enthusiastically
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'What's my name again?' is performative mock-uncertainty — fishing for the affirmation he just admitted he needs
jokes.explanation: A nice button to the sofa joke — Larry immediately performs the exact behavior he just confessed to (seeking crowd attention). The self-awareness layered over the self-centeredness is very Larry. Works best as an extension of joke 54.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I gave him that whole manager/agent shit. And he bought it?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Of course. He said it was his manager and agent?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's what he told me. You bought that horseshit?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Are you kidding?

jokes.text: Artie on not wanting to talk to Spade: 'You don't wanna talk to the little prick?' Larry: 'No.' Artie: 'Good.'
jokes.setup: Artie relays that Spade wants to come explain himself.
jokes.punchline: Artie's casual 'Good' after Larry refuses suggests he's fully on Larry's side and had no interest in a reconciliation himself. The exchange is three words and complete.
jokes.explanation: Economy is the whole joke — 'Good.' as Artie's complete and enthusiastic agreement. The beat is tiny but the Artie-Larry alliance is efficiently reinforced. Rip Torn making 'Good' sound like a declaration of war is performance-dependent but the writing sets it up well.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: We'll bump him a few times. He'll get the message. Little rat prick.

jokes.text: Me and my cold Vulcan logic.
jokes.setup: Artie has just made a practical decision about the Spade situation; the Shatner/Star Trek sketch is in prep nearby
jokes.punchline: Artie applies 'cold Vulcan logic' to himself — a Shatner/Star Trek reference used to describe his own ruthless pragmatism
jokes.explanation: A lovely piece of show-runner self-characterization — Artie borrowing Star Trek terminology to describe his own philosophy. The callback is organic (Shatner is in the building; the sketch is being prepped). Very good economy.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Like anyone goes, 'Oh, he's good. He's good. Love his work.'

jokes.text: Knock, knock. / Who's there? / What do you mean? / You said, 'Knock, knock.' / No, I was just... I was just saying that. / But you said, 'Knock, knock' when you came in. / Right. / Who's there? / Hank. / Hank who? / Hank Kingsley. / Come in.
jokes.setup: Hank knocks and says 'knock, knock' while entering Larry's office; Larry responds as if it's a knock-knock joke
jokes.punchline: The miscommunication escalates into a full, tortured knock-knock joke where the punchline is simply Hank's name — completely anti-climactic — culminating in Larry's 'Come in' when Hank is already in the room
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's finest moments — a sustained anti-joke that works by frustrating the knock-knock joke format completely. Hank's genuine confusion, Larry's pedantic insistence on following the format through to its conclusion, and the utterly flat punchline ('Hank Kingsley') followed by 'Come in' (when Hank is ALREADY in the room) creates a perfect comedy of errors. The structure is meticulous. The anticlimactic payoff IS the joke. High marks across the board — this is original, character-specific (only Hank and Larry would get stuck in this loop), and structurally elegant in its anti-structure.

jokes.text: I mean, you remember the first time you did The Tonight Show? / How do you think Merv felt?
jokes.setup: Hank is gently challenging Larry's decision to ban Spade, using Larry's own career history as a mirror
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'How do you think Merv felt?' — the implication that Larry is now the Merv Griffin in this situation (the established host being undercut by an ambitious young comedian)
jokes.explanation: A thematically rich joke that works as both comedy and character revelation. Hank — who usually lacks insight — here lands a genuinely stinging observation: Larry IS Merv in this scenario. The reversal is satisfying and uncomfortable. The economy is excellent. This gives Hank an unusual moment of actual wisdom, which makes it funnier and more poignant.

jokes.text: But Merv was on in the afternoon. Johnny was on at night. There wasn't a conflict. I don't think the unspoken rule applied.
jokes.setup: Hank has just suggested Larry was equally guilty of doing Merv before The Tonight Show
jokes.punchline: Larry's elaborate rationalization for why his situation was totally different — the afternoon/night distinction as a moral loophole — is desperate self-justification that he clearly doesn't believe
jokes.explanation: Larry's technical legalism about the 'unspoken rule' — parsed by time slot — is a great character moment. He's essentially arguing that his own version of the same transgression was technically exempt because of scheduling. The hypocrisy is the joke, and it's delivered with conviction.

jokes.text: But Merv gave you your start, right? / [Larry's reaction — he goes to get the girls to end the conversation]
jokes.setup: Hank has cornered Larry logically — Merv gave Larry his start, just as Larry gave Spade his
jokes.punchline: Larry doesn't answer — instead he immediately calls for 'the girls' to end the conversation. The dodge IS the joke — the guilty pivot.
jokes.explanation: Larry's non-answer is the punchline. His pivot to 'Where are the girls, Hank?' in response to a question he cannot answer is perfect — the guilty silence is more revealing than any dialogue. A great example of The Larry Sanders Show's strength: the comedy lives in what characters won't say. High character integration.

jokes.text: It's just I don't expect you to totally forgive me or not think I'm an asshole for what I did, but honestly, my manager and my agent — I went over it with them, and they said it would be fine.
jokes.setup: Spade has come to Larry's office to apologize/explain the Tonight Show situation
jokes.punchline: Spade's 'manager and agent said it would be fine' defense — the standard showbiz deflection of personal responsibility onto representation
jokes.explanation: A recognizable industry excuse that functions as character comedy — Spade deflecting to management is both believable and slightly cowardly, which is the joke. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: That is not true. I happened to have started on Merv. Merv gave me a few good shots before I did The Tonight Show. That's a fact. / Jesus, Merv must have been pissed off. / He was not pissed off. They were on at different times of the day.
jokes.setup: Spade has pointed out that Larry's situation with Merv Griffin mirrors what Spade did to Larry
jokes.punchline: Larry wheels out the afternoon/night defense AGAIN for Spade — having used it on Hank — and Spade's 'Jesus, Merv must have been pissed off' is the perfect needle-prick
jokes.explanation: A layered callback that delivers on multiple threads — Spade puncturing Larry's rationalizations with a completely direct 'Jesus, Merv must have been pissed off' is devastating, and Larry's repeat of the afternoon/night defense makes him look even more absurd the second time around. Excellent structural payoff for the episode's thematic throughline.

jokes.text: Look, we'll let a couple months go by, let things settle down, and then we'll book you again on the show, okay? / That'd be great. That's very generous.
jokes.setup: Larry appears to be making peace with Spade and offering to re-book him
jokes.punchline: The audience knows (from the earlier meeting) that Larry and Artie have already decided to 'bump him a few times until he gets the message' — Spade's sincere 'That's very generous' lands with dramatic irony
jokes.explanation: The joke only works because we already know the plan — Larry's magnanimity is entirely fake, and Spade's grateful 'That's very generous' lands as a painful irony. The gap between what Larry says and what he means is the show's central comic engine, and this scene illustrates it perfectly. Strong dramatic irony structure.

jokes.text: Thanks, Mr. Sanders. / Hey, call me... / You want me to call you? / I was gonna say, 'Call me Larry.'
jokes.setup: Spade is leaving after what he believes was a successful reconciliation
jokes.punchline: Spade's 'You want me to call you?' mishears 'Call me Larry' as an invitation to literally phone Larry — another awkward miscommunication that echoes the 'So long/Long?' exchange earlier
jokes.explanation: A structural callback to the earlier miscommunication with Spade — these two can't even end a conversation cleanly. The 'You want me to call you?' beat extends the fake-warmth joke: even the casual sign-off is a minefield. The parallel with the Mustang/So Long scene gives it extra resonance on rewatch.

jokes.text: How did it go? / Good. I gave him that whole manager/agent shit. / And he bought it? / Of course.
jokes.setup: Larry reports back to Artie on the Spade meeting
jokes.punchline: Larry reveals he used the 'manager/agent' excuse to placate Spade — the same excuse Spade used on Larry — making Larry just as cynical and duplicitous as Spade was
jokes.explanation: The episode's thematic and comedic peak — Larry fed Spade the exact same line Spade used on him. The symmetry is perfect: Larry condemned Spade for deflecting blame to management, then uses the same technique to manipulate Spade. The self-awareness is zero. This is the show's central thesis: everyone in Hollywood is equally fake and everyone thinks they're uniquely sincere. Among the episode's best-constructed moments — it retroactively recontextualizes the entire Spade plot.

jokes.text: He said it was his manager and agent? / That's what he told me. / You bought that horseshit? / Are you kidding? I told him we'd wait a couple months, and then we'd book him again. We'll bump him a few times. He'll get the message.
jokes.setup: Artie is incredulous that Spade blamed his management; Larry clarifies he didn't believe it
jokes.punchline: Larry's full plan revealed — the 'months to wait' offer is fake; he'll bump Spade repeatedly until the message is clear. The cynicism beneath the warmth is complete.
jokes.explanation: The full reveal of Larry's scheme makes the previous scene retroactively funnier. Artie's 'You bought that horseshit?' is a great Artie line. The plan — bump him until he gets the message — is petty enough to be perfectly Larry. This scene and joke 65 work best as a unit.

jokes.text: Larry, Arthur, we have a huge problem. Joe Pesci just cancelled. What are we gonna do now?
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie have just concluded their revenge plan against Spade with great satisfaction
jokes.punchline: Immediate new crisis — Joe Pesci has cancelled, eliminating one of their major guests. The satisfaction of resolving one problem is instantly punctured by a new, possibly worse one.
jokes.explanation: A classic sitcom structural beat — the characters' brief moment of triumph instantly undercut by the next crisis. Works as escalating chaos. The specific choice of Joe Pesci (given earlier context about Spade) is a neat irony.

jokes.text: David Spade performs the airline material on The Larry Sanders Show — the same material he performed on Leno, the same material he previewed in the office.
jokes.setup: We've now heard this exact airline material three times: previewed in the office, performed on Leno, and now performed on The Larry Sanders Show
jokes.punchline: The triple repetition itself is the joke — the audience now knows the punchlines before Spade delivers them, and Larry is forced to sit and smile at material he's already found professionally offensive
jokes.explanation: The triple-repetition payoff is structurally bold. By the third airing, the audience laughs not at Spade's material (which they now know) but at the meta-situation: Larry is forced to host the exact comedian doing the exact material that caused the whole crisis. Brilliant sustained comedy architecture. The fact that Spade is doing the same jokes is both the setup and the punchline.

jokes.text: David Spade performs his airline material on The Larry Sanders Show — the exact same set he did on Leno the night before, which started the entire conflict.
jokes.setup: After all the scheming, Spade appears on the show and begins his set
jokes.punchline: He opens with the pilot name joke — the same material that caused the entire episode's conflict — as the episode closes. The circle is complete: nothing has changed, no lesson was learned
jokes.explanation: The final joke of the episode is structural and meta: we hear the same material for the third time, now from the Larry Sanders Show stage, completing a triple callback. The comedy is entirely in the recognition — this is the material that blew up everyone's lives, and here it is again, being performed exactly as planned, as if nothing happened. Pure Larry Sanders nihilism: the show goes on regardless. Marked is_standup true because it's an in-world performance, though its function as a structural callback is the real comedic achievement.

tmdb_overview: Larry is annoyed that David Spade is booked on another show and Hank's fan club visits.
